idiom_name: LINQ to XML functional construction (XElement) / XslCompiledTransform
implementation_notes: In C# the transformer class collapses into System.Xml.Linq functional construction: new XElement("li", value) nests elements and escapes text and attributes automatically, LINQ queries over the tree cover the selection logic, and XElement.WriteTo(XmlWriter) or ToString() serializes. XslCompiledTransform is the declarative route - Load compiles a stylesheet once, Transform runs it into an XmlWriter or stream. The classic Transformer object remains justified when the output is HTML text with conditionals that a tree-building expression would obscure.
pitfalls: XmlWriter emits what it is told but validates little: writing HTML through it requires the XHTML namespace, otherwise every element carries an xmlns attribute.
XslCompiledTransform compiles inside Load and requires dynamic code generation; cache the compiled instance instead of loading per request.
XSLT scripting and the document() function are disabled by default: enabling them on untrusted stylesheets lets a stylesheet read local files and reach the network.

variants.name: XslCompiledTransform stylesheet
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative realization on .NET: xslt.Load("view.xsl") compiles once, xslt.Transform(input, XmlWriter) applies it, XsltArgumentList passes per-request parameters and XsltSettings keeps scripting disabled. Choose it when presentation is a stylesheet artifact maintained separately from application code and the input can be shaped as XML.
pitfalls: XSLT 1.0 only: XSLT 2.0/3.0 features are unavailable, so complex presentation logic must not be designed around them.
Transform is not thread-safe against concurrent calls on the same XslCompiledTransform instance with a shared XsltArgumentList; use one argument list per request.
